name: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
credit: Imagined portrait by Kahlil Gibran (1917), no contemporary likeness exists · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri (973–1057) was a blind poet, philosopher and sceptic born in Ma'arrat al-Nu'man in northern Syria. Blinded by smallpox in childhood, he studied in Aleppo and Antioch, spent a short period in Baghdad, and returned to his home town, where he lived for decades as a celebrated ascetic and teacher, a vegetarian who called himself a prisoner of three things: blindness, solitude and the body. His verse questions revelation, priestly authority and the claims of every rival creed, and he has often been called the Voltaire or Lucretius of the Arabs.

His two great collections are Saqt al-zand (Sparks of the Tinder) and the Luzum ma la yalzam (The Necessity of What Is Not Necessary), the latter known as the Luzumiyat. The poems here are from Ameen Rihani's 1918 English version, a free rendering in quatrains selected from those books; they follow the sense and spirit of the Arabic rather than its form, which is monorhymed and in a different metre.

poems.title: The sable wings of Night pursuing day
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The sable wings of Night pursuing day
Across the opalescent hills, display
The wondrous star-gems which the fiery suns
Are scattering upon their fiery way.

poems.title: O my Companion, Night is passing fair
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
O my Companion, Night is passing fair,
Fairer than aught the dawn and sundown wear;
And fairer, too, than all the gilded days
Of blond Illusion and its golden snare.

poems.title: Hark, in the minarets muazzens call
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Hark, in the minarets muazzens call
The evening hour that in the interval
Of darkness Ahmad might remembered be,--
Remembered of the Darkness be they all.

poems.title: And hear the others who with cymbals try
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And hear the others who with cymbals try
To stay the feet of every passer-by:
The market-men along the darkling lane
Are crying up their wares.--Oh! let them cry.

poems.title: Mohammed or Messiah! Hear thou me
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Mohammed or Messiah! Hear thou me,
The truth entire nor here nor there can be;
How should our God who made the sun and moon
Give all his light to One, I cannot see.

poems.title: Come, let us with the naked Night now rest
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Come, let us with the naked Night now rest
And read in Allah's Book the sonnet best:
The Pleiads--ah, the Moon from them departs,--
She draws her veil and hastens toward the west.

poems.title: The Pleiads follow; and our Ethiop Queen
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The Pleiads follow; and our Ethiop Queen,
Emerging from behind her starry screen,
Will steep her tresses in the saffron dye
Of dawn, and vanish in the morning sheen.

poems.title: The secret of the day and night is in
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The secret of the day and night is in
The constellations, which forever spin
Around each other in the comet-dust;--
The comet-dust and humankind are kin.

poems.title: But whether of dust or fire or foam, the glaive
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
But whether of dust or fire or foam, the glaive
Of Allah cleaves the planet and the wave
Of this mysterious Heaven-Sea of life,
And lo! we have the Cradle of the Grave.

poems.title: The Grave and Cradle, the untiring twain
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The Grave and Cradle, the untiring twain,
Who in the markets of this narrow lane
Bordered of darkness, ever give and take
In equal measure--what's the loss or gain?

poems.title: Ay, like the circles which the sun doth spin
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Ay, like the circles which the sun doth spin
Of gossamer, we end as we begin;
Our feet are on the heads of those that pass,
But ever their Graves around our Cradles grin.

poems.title: And what avails it then that Man be born
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And what avails it then that Man be born
To joy or sorrow?--why rejoice or mourn?
The doling doves are calling to the rose;
The dying rose is bleeding o'er the thorn.

poems.title: And he the Messenger, who takes away
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And he the Messenger, who takes away
The faded garments, purple, white, and gray
Of all our dreams unto the Dyer, will
Bring back new robes to-morrow--so they say.

poems.title: But now the funeral is passing by
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
But now the funeral is passing by,
And in its trail, beneath this moaning sky,
The howdaj comes,--both vanish into night;
To me are one, the sob, the joyous cry.

poems.title: With tombs and ruined temples groans the land
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
With tombs and ruined temples groans the land
In which our forbears in the drifting sand
Arise as dunes upon the track of Time
To mark the cycles of the moving hand

poems.title: Of Fate. Alas! and we shall follow soon
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Of Fate. Alas! and we shall follow soon
Into the night eternal or the noon;
The wayward daughters of the spheres return
Unto the bosom of their sun or moon.

poems.title: And from the last days of Thamud and 'Ad
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And from the last days of Thamud and 'Ad
Up to the first of Hashem's fearless lad,
Who smashed the idols of his mighty tribe,
What idols and what heroes Death has had!

poems.title: Tread lightly, for the mighty that have been
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Tread lightly, for the mighty that have been
Might now be breathing in the dust unseen;
Lightly, the violets beneath thy feet
Spring from the mole of some Arabian queen.

poems.title: Many a grave embraces friend and foe
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Many a grave embraces friend and foe
Behind the curtain of this sorry show
Of love and hate inscrutable; alas!
The Fates will always reap the while they sow.

poems.title: The silken fibre of the fell Zakkum
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The silken fibre of the fell Zakkum,
As warp and woof, is woven on the loom
Of life into a tapestry of dreams
To decorate the chariot-seat of Doom.

poems.title: And still we weave, and still we are content
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And still we weave, and still we are content
In slaving for the sovereigns who have spent
The savings of the toiling of the mind
Upon the glory of Dismemberment.

poems.title: Nor king nor slave the hungry Days will spare
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Nor king nor slave the hungry Days will spare;
Between their fangéd Hours alike we fare:
Anon they bound upon us while we play
Unheeding at the threshold of their Lair.

poems.title: Then Jannat or Juhannam? From the height
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Then Jannat or Juhannam? From the height
Of reason I can see nor fire nor light
That feeds not on the darknesses; we pass
From world to world, like shadows through the night.

poems.title: Or sleep--and shall it be eternal sleep
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Or sleep--and shall it be eternal sleep
Somewhither in the bosom of the deep
Infinities of cosmic dust, or here
Where gracile cypresses the vigil keep!

poems.title: Upon the threshing-floor of life I burn
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Upon the threshing-floor of life I burn
Beside the Winnower a word to learn;
And only this: Man's of the soil and sun,
And to the soil and sun he shall return.

poems.title: And like a spider's house or sparrow's nest
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And like a spider's house or sparrow's nest,
The Sultan's palace, though upon the crest
Of glory's mountain, soon or late must go:
Ay, all abodes to ruin are addrest.

poems.title: So, too, the creeds of Man: the one prevails
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
So, too, the creeds of Man: the one prevails
Until the other comes; and this one fails
When that one triumphs; ay, the lonesome world
Will always want the latest fairy-tales.

poems.title: Seek not the Tavern of Belief, my friend
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Seek not the Tavern of Belief, my friend,
Until the Sakis there their morals mend;
A lie imbibed a thousand lies will breed,
And thou'lt become a Saki in the end.

poems.title: By fearing whom I trust I find my way
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
By fearing whom I trust I find my way
To truth; by trusting wholly I betray
The trust of wisdom; better far is doubt
Which brings the false into the light of day.

poems.title: Or wilt thou commerce have with those who make
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Or wilt thou commerce have with those who make
Rugs of the rainbow, rainbows of the snake,
Snakes of a staff, and other wondrous things?--
The burning thirst a mirage can not slake.

poems.title: Religion is a maiden veiled in prayer
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Religion is a maiden veiled in prayer,
Whose bridal gifts and dowry those who care
Can buy in Mutakallem's shop of words
But I for such, a dirham can not spare.

poems.title: Why linger here, why turn another page
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Why linger here, why turn another page?
Oh! seal with doubt the whole book of the age;
Doubt every one, even him, the seeming slave
Of righteousness, and doubt the canting sage.

poems.title: Some day the weeping daughters of Hadil
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Some day the weeping daughters of Hadil
Will say unto the bulbuls: "Let's appeal
To Allah in behalf of Brother Man
Who's at the mercy now of Ababil."

poems.title: Of Ababil! I would the tale were true
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Of Ababil! I would the tale were true,--
Would all the birds were such winged furies too;
The scourging and the purging were a boon
For me, O my dear Brothers, and for you.

poems.title: Methinks Allah divides me to complete
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Methinks Allah divides me to complete
His problem, which with Xs is replete;
For I am free and I am too in chains
Groping along the labyrinthine street.

poems.title: And round the Well how oft my Soul doth grope
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And round the Well how oft my Soul doth grope
Athirst; but lo! my Bucket hath no Rope:
I cry for water, and the deep, dark Well
Echoes my wailing cry, but not my hope.

poems.title: Ah, many have I seen of those who fell
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Ah, many have I seen of those who fell
While drawing, with a swagger, from the Well;
They came with Rope and Bucket, and they went
Empty of hand another tale to tell.

poems.title: The I in me standing upon the brink
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The I in me standing upon the brink
Would leap into the Well to get a drink;
But how to rise once in the depth, I cry,
And cowardly behind my logic slink.

poems.title: And she: "How long must I the burden bear
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And she: "How long must I the burden bear?
How long this tattered garment must I wear?"
And I: "Why wear it? Leave it here, and go
Away without it--little do I care."

poems.title: But once when we were quarreling, the door
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
But once when we were quarreling, the door
Was opened by a Visitor who bore
Both Rope and Pail; he offered them and said:
"Drink, if you will, but once, and nevermore."

poems.title: One draught, more bitter than the Zakkum tree
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
One draught, more bitter than the Zakkum tree,
Brought us unto the land of mystery
Where rising Sand and Dust and Flame conceal
The door of every Caravanseri.

poems.title: We reach a door and there the legend find
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
We reach a door and there the legend find.
"To all the Pilgrims of the Human Mind:
Knock and pass on!" We knock and knock and knock;
But no one answers save the moaning wind.

poems.title: How like a door the knowledge we attain
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
How like a door the knowledge we attain,
Which door is on the bourne of the Inane;
It opens and our nothingness is closed,--
It closes and in darkness we remain.

poems.title: Hither we come unknowing, hence we go
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri

poems.title: Apply thy wit, O Brother, here and there
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Apply thy wit, O Brother, here and there
Upon this and upon that; but beware
Lest in the end--ah, better at the start
Go to the Tinker for a slight repair.

poems.title: And why so much ado, and wherefore lay
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And why so much ado, and wherefore lay
The burden of the years upon the day
Of thy vain dreams? Who polishes his sword
Morning and eve will polish it away.

poems.title: I heard it whispered in the cryptic streets
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
I heard it whispered in the cryptic streets
Where every sage the same dumb shadow meets:
"We are but words fallen from the lipe of Time
Which God, that we might understand, repeats."

poems.title: Another said: "The creeping worm hath shown
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Another said: "The creeping worm hath shown,
In her discourse on human flesh and bone,
That Man was once the bed on which she slept--
The walking dust was once a thing of stone."

poems.title: And still another: "We are coins which fade
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And still another: "We are coins which fade
In circulation, coins which Allah made
To cheat Iblis: the good and bad alike
Are spent by Fate upon a passing shade."

poems.title: And in the pottery the potter cried
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And in the pottery the potter cried,
As on his work shone all the master's pride--
"How is it, Rabbi, I, thy slave, can make
Such vessels as nobody dare deride?"

poems.title: The Earth then spake: "My children silent be
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The Earth then spake: "My children silent be;
Same are to God the camel and the flea:
He makes a mess of me to nourish you,
Then makes a mess of you to nourish me."

poems.title: Now, I believe the Potter will essay
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Now, I believe the Potter will essay
Once more the Wheel, and from a better clay
Will make a better Vessel, and perchance
A masterpiece which will endure for aye.

poems.title: With better skill he even will remould
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
With better skill he even will remould
The scattered potsherds of the New and Old;
Then you and I will not disdain to buy,
Though in the mart of Iblis they be sold.

poems.title: Sooth I have told the masters of the mart
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Sooth I have told the masters of the mart
Of rusty creeds and Babylonian art
Of magic. Now the truth about myself--
Here is the secret of my wincing heart.

poems.title: I muse, but in my musings I recall
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
I muse, but in my musings I recall
The days of my iniquity; we're all--
An arrow shot across the wilderness,
Somewhither, in the wilderness must fall.

poems.title: I laugh, but in my laughter-cup I pour
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
I laugh, but in my laughter-cup I pour
The tears of scorn and melancholy sore;
I who am shattered by the hand of Doubt,
Like glass to be remoulded nevermore.

poems.title: I wheedle, too, even like my slave Zeidun
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
I wheedle, too, even like my slave Zeidun,
Who robs at dawn his brother, and at noon
Prostrates himself in prayer--ah, let us pray
That Night might blot us and our sins, and soon.

poems.title: But in the fatal coils, without intent
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
But in the fatal coils, without intent,
We sin; wherefore a future punishment?
They say the metal dead a deadly steel
Becomes with Allah's knowledge and consent.

poems.title: And even the repentant sinner's tear
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And even the repentant sinner's tear
Falling into Juhannam's very ear,
Goes to its heart, extinguishes its fire
For ever and forever,--so I hear.

poems.title: Between the white and purple Words of Time
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Between the white and purple Words of Time
In motley garb with Destiny I rhyme:
The colored glasses to the water give
The colors of a symbolry sublime.

poems.title: How oft, when young, my brothers I would shun
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
How oft, when young, my brothers I would shun
If their religious feelings were not spun
Of my own cobweb, which I find was but
A spider's revelation of the sun.

poems.title: Now, mosques and churches--even a Kaaba Stone
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Now, mosques and churches--even a Kaaba Stone,
Korans and Bibles--even a martyr's bone,--
All these and more my heart can tolerate,
For my religion's love, and love alone.

poems.title: To humankind, O Brother, consecrate
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
To humankind, O Brother, consecrate
Thy heart, and shun the hundred Sects that prate
About the things they little know about--
Let all receive thy pity, none thy hate.

poems.title: The tavern and the temple also shun
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The tavern and the temple also shun,
For sheikh and libertine in sooth are one;
And when the pious knave begins to pule,
The knave in purple breaks his vow anon.

poems.title: "The wine's forbidden," say these honest folk
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
"The wine's forbidden," say these honest folk,
But for themselves the law they will revoke;
The snivelling sheikh says he's without a garb,
When in the tap-house he had pawned his cloak.

poems.title: Or in the house of lust. The priestly name
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Or in the house of lust. The priestly name
And priestly turban once were those of Shame--
And Shame is preaching in the pulpit now--
If pulpits tumble down, I'm not to blame.

poems.title: For after she declaims upon the vows
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
For after she declaims upon the vows
Of Faith, she pusillanimously bows
Before the Sultan's wine-empurpled throne,
While he and all his courtezans carouse.

poems.title: Carouse, ye sovereign lords! The wheel will roll
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Carouse, ye sovereign lords! The wheel will roll
Forever to confound and to console:
Who sips to-day the golden cup will drink
Mayhap to-morrow in a wooden bowl--

poems.title: And silent drink. The tumult of our mirth
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And silent drink. The tumult of our mirth
Is worse than our mad welcoming of birth:--
The thunder hath a grandeur, but the rains,
Without the thunder, quench the thirst of Earth.

poems.title: The Prophets, too, among us come to teach
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The Prophets, too, among us come to teach,
Are one with those who from the pulpit preach;
They pray, and slay, and pass away, and yet
Our ills are as the pebbles on the beach.

poems.title: And though around the temple they should run
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And though around the temple they should run
For seventy times and seven, and in the sun
Of mad devotion drool, their prayers are still
Like their desires of feasting-fancies spun.

poems.title: Oh! let them in the marshes grope, or ride
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Oh! let them in the marshes grope, or ride
Their jaded Myths along the mountain-side;
Come up with me, O Brother, to the heights
Where Reason is the prophet and the guide.

poems.title: "What is thy faith and creed," they ask of me
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
"What is thy faith and creed," they ask of me,
"And who art thou? Unseal thy pedigree."--
I am the child of Time, my tribe, mankind,
And now this world's my caravanseri.

poems.title: Swathe thee in wool, my Sufi friend, and go
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Swathe thee in wool, my Sufi friend, and go
Thy way; in cotton I the wiser grow;
But we ourselves are shreds of earth, and soon
The Tailor of the Universe will sew.

poems.title: Ay! suddenly the mystic Hand will seal
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Ay! suddenly the mystic Hand will seal
The saint's devotion and the sinner's weal;
They worship Saturn, but I worship One
Before whom Saturn and the Heavens kneel.

poems.title: Among the crumbling ruins of the creeds
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Among the crumbling ruins of the creeds
The Scout upon his camel played his reeds
And called out to his people,--"Let us hence!
The pasture here is full of noxious weeds."

poems.title: Among us falsehood is proclaimed aloud
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Among us falsehood is proclaimed aloud,
But truth is whispered to the phantom bowed
Of conscience; ay! and Wrong is ever crowned,
While Right and Reason are denied a shroud.

poems.title: And why in this dark Kingdom tribute pay
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And why in this dark Kingdom tribute pay?
With clamant multitudes why stop to pray?
Oh! hear the inner Voice:--"If thou'lt be right,
Do what they deem is wrong, and go thy way."

poems.title: Thy way unto the Sun the spaces through
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Thy way unto the Sun the spaces through
Where king Orion's black-eyed huris slew
The Mother of Night to guide the Wings that bear
The flame divine hid in a drop of dew.

poems.title: Hear ye who in the dust of ages creep
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Hear ye who in the dust of ages creep,
And in the halls of wicked masters sleep:--
Arise! and out of this wan weariness
Where Allah's laughter makes the Devil weep.

poems.title: Arise! for lo! the Laughter and the Weeping
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Arise! for lo! the Laughter and the Weeping
Reveal the Weapon which the Master's keeping
Above your heads; Oh! take it up and strike!
The lion of tyranny is only sleeping.

poems.title: Evil and Virtue? Shadows on the street
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Evil and Virtue? Shadows on the street
Of Fate and Vanity,--but shadows meet
When in the gloaming they are hast'ning forth
To drink with Night annihilation sweet.

poems.title: And thus the Sun will write and will efface
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And thus the Sun will write and will efface
The mystic symbols which the sages trace
In vain, for all the worlds of God are stored
In his enduring vessels Time and Space.

poems.title: For all my learning's but a veil, I guess
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
For all my learning's but a veil, I guess,
Veiling the phantom of my nothingness;
Howbeit, there are those who think me wise,
And those who think me--even these I bless.

poems.title: And all my years, as vapid as my lay
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And all my years, as vapid as my lay,
Are bitter morsels of a mystic day,--
The day of Fate, who carries in his lap
December snows and snow-white flowers of May.

poems.title: Allah, my sleep is woven through, it seems
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri

poems.title: The subtle ways of Destiny I know
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The subtle ways of Destiny I know;
In me she plays her game of "Give and Go."
Misfortune I receive in cash, but joy,
In drafts on Heaven or on the winds that blow.

poems.title: I give and go, grim Destiny,--I play
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
I give and go, grim Destiny,--I play
Upon this checker-board of Night and Day
The dark game with thee, but the day will come
When one will turn the Board the other way.

poems.title: If my house-swallow, laboring with zest
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
If my house-swallow, laboring with zest,
Felt like myself the burden of unrest,
Unlightened by inscrutable designs,
She would not build her young that cozy nest.

poems.title: Thy life with guiltless life-blood do not stain
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Thy life with guiltless life-blood do not stain--
Hunt not the children of the woods; in vain
Thou'lt try one day to wash thy bloody hand:
Nor hunter here nor hunted long remain.

poems.title: Oh! cast my dust away from thee, and doff
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Oh! cast my dust away from thee, and doff
Thy cloak of sycophancy and like stuff:
I'm but a shadow on the sandy waste,--
Enough of thy duplicity, enough!

poems.title: Behold! the Veil that hid thy soul is torn
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Behold! the Veil that hid thy soul is torn
And all thy secrets on the winds are borne:
The hand of Sin has written on thy face
"Awake, for these untimely furrows warn!"

poems.title: A prince of souls, 'tis sung in ancient lay
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
A prince of souls, 'tis sung in ancient lay,
One morning sought a vesture of the clay;
He came into the Pottery, the fool--
The lucky fool was warned to stay away.

poems.title: But I was not. Oh! that the Fates decree
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
But I was not. Oh! that the Fates decree
That I now cast aside this clay of me;
My soul and body wedded for a while
Are sick and would that separation be.

poems.title: "Thou shalt not kill!"--Thy words, O God, we heed
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
"Thou shalt not kill!"--Thy words, O God, we heed,
Though thy two Soul-devouring Angels feed
Thy Promise of another life on this,--
To have spared us both, it were a boon indeed.

poems.title: Oh! that some one would but return to tell
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Oh! that some one would but return to tell
If old Nubakht is burning now in hell,
Or if the workers for the Prophet's prize
Are laughing at his Paradisal sell.

poems.title: Once I have tried to string a few Pearl-seeds
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Once I have tried to string a few Pearl-seeds
Upon my Rosary of wooden beads;
But I have searched, and I have searched in vain
For pearls in all the caverns of the creeds

poems.title: And in the palaces of wealth I found
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And in the palaces of wealth I found
Some beads of wisdom scattered on the ground,
Around the throne of Power, beneath the feet
Of fair-faced slaves with flowers of folly crowned.

poems.title: Thy wealth can shed no tears around thy bier
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Thy wealth can shed no tears around thy bier,
Nor can it wash thy hands of shame and fear;
Ere thou departest with it freely part,--
Let others plead for thee and God will hear.

poems.title: For me thy silks and feathers have no charm
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
For me thy silks and feathers have no charm
The pillow I like best is my right arm;
The comforts of this passing show I spurn,
For Poverty can do the soul no harm.

poems.title: The guiding hand of Allah I can see
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The guiding hand of Allah I can see
Upon my staff: of what use then is he
Who'd be the blind man's guide? Thou silent oak,
No son of Eve shall walk with me and thee.

poems.title: My life's the road on which I blindly speed
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
My life's the road on which I blindly speed:
My goal's the grave on which I plant a reed
To shape my Hope, but soon the Hand unseen
Will strike, and lo! I'm but a sapless weed.

poems.title: O Rabbi, curse us not if we have been
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
O Rabbi, curse us not if we have been
Nursed in the shadow of the Gate of Sin
Built by thy hand--yea, ev'n thine angels blink
When we are coming out and going in.

poems.title: And like the dead of Ind I do not fear
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And like the dead of Ind I do not fear
To go to thee in flames; the most austere
Angel of fire a softer tooth and tongue
Hath he than dreadful Munker and Nakir.

poems.title: Now, at this end of Adam's line I stand
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Now, at this end of Adam's line I stand
Holding my father's life-curse in my hand,
Doing no one the wrong that he did me:--
Ah, would that he were barren as the sand!

poems.title: Ay, thus thy children, though they sovereigns be
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Ay, thus thy children, though they sovereigns be,
When truth upon them dawns, will turn on thee,
Who cast them into life's dark labyrinth
Where even old Izrail can not see.

poems.title: And in the labyrinth both son and sire
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And in the labyrinth both son and sire
Awhile will fan and fuel hatred's fire;
Sparks of the log of evil are all men
Allwhere--extinguished be the race entire!

poems.title: If miracles were wrought in ancient years
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
If miracles were wrought in ancient years,
Why not to-day, O Heaven-cradled seers?
The highway's strewn with dead, the lepers weep,
If ye but knew,--if ye but saw their tears!

poems.title: Fan thou a lisping fire and it will leap
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Fan thou a lisping fire and it will leap
In flames, but dost thou fan an ashy heap?
They would respond, indeed, whom thou dost call,
Were they not dead, alas! or dead asleep.

poems.title: The way of vice is open as the sky
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The way of vice is open as the sky,
The way of virtue's like the needle's eye;
But whether here or there, the eager Soul
Has only two Companions--Whence and Why.

poems.title: Whence come, O firmament, thy myriad lights
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Whence come, O firmament, thy myriad lights?
Whence comes thy sap, O vineyard of the heights?
Whence comes the perfume of the rose, and whence
The spirit-larva which the body blights?

poems.title: Whence does the nettle get its bitter sting
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Whence does the nettle get its bitter sting?
Whence do the honey bees their honey bring?
Whence our Companions, too--our Whence and Why?
O Soul, I do not know a single thing!

poems.title: How many like us in the ages past
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
How many like us in the ages past
Have blindly soared, though like a pebble cast,
Seeking the veil of mystery to tear,
But fell accurst beneath the burning blast?

poems.title: Why try to con the book of earth and sky
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Why try to con the book of earth and sky,
Why seek the truth which neither you nor I
Can grasp? But Death methinks the secret keeps,
And will impart it to us by and by.

poems.title: The Sultan, too, relinquishing his throne
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The Sultan, too, relinquishing his throne
Must wayfare through the darkening dust alone
Where neither crown nor kingdom be, and he,
Part of the Secret, here and there is blown.

poems.title: To clay the mighty Sultan must return
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
To clay the mighty Sultan must return
And, chancing, help a praying slave to burn
His midnight oil before the face of Him,
Who of the Sultan makes an incense urn.

poems.title: Turned to a cup, who once the sword of state
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Turned to a cup, who once the sword of state
Held o'er the head of slave and potentate,
Is now held in the tippler's trembling hand,
Or smashed upon the tavern-floor of Fate.

poems.title: For this I say, Be watchful of the Cage
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
For this I say, Be watchful of the Cage
Of chance; it opes alike to fool and sage;
Spy on the moment, for to-morrow'll be,
Like yesterday, an obliterated page.

poems.title: Yea, kiss the rosy cheeks of new-born Day
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Yea, kiss the rosy cheeks of new-born Day,
And hail eternity in every ray
Forming a halo round its infant head,
Illumining thy labyrinthine way.

poems.title: But I, the thrice-imprisoned, try to troll
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
But I, the thrice-imprisoned, try to troll
Strains of the song of night, which fill with dole
My blindness, my confinement, and my flesh--
The sordid habitation of my soul.

poems.title: Howbeit, my inner vision heir shall be
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Howbeit, my inner vision heir shall be
To the increasing flames of mystery
Which may illumine yet my prisons all,
And crown the ever living hope of me.

poems.title: Quatrain I
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Abandon worship in the mosque and shrink
  From idle prayer, from sacrificial sheep,
  For Destiny will bring the bowl of sleep
Or bowl of tribulation--you shall drink.

poems.title: Quatrain II
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The scarlet eyes of Morning are pursued
  By Night, who growls along the narrow lane;
  But as they crash upon our world the twain
Devour us and are strengthened for the feud.

poems.title: Quatrain III
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Vain are your dreams of marvellous emprise,
  Vainly you sail among uncharted spaces,
  Vainly seek harbour in this world of faces
If it has been determined otherwise.

poems.title: Quatrain IV
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Behold, my friends, there is reserved for me
  The splendour of our traffic with the sky:
  You pay your court to Saturn, whereas I
Am slain by One far mightier than he.

poems.title: Quatrain V
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
You that must travel with a weary load
  Along this darkling, labyrinthine street--
  Have men with torches at your head and feet
If you would pass the dangers of the road.

poems.title: Quatrain VI
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
So shall you find all armour incomplete
  And open to the whips of circumstance,
  That so shall you be girdled of mischance
Till you be folded in the winding-sheet.

poems.title: Quatrain VII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Have conversation with the wind that goes
  Bearing a pack of loveliness and pain:
  The golden exultation of the grain
And the last, sacred whisper of the rose

poems.title: Quatrain VIII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
But if in some enchanted garden bloom
  The rose imperial that will not fade,
  Ah! shall I go with desecrating spade
And underneath her glories build a tomb?

poems.title: Quatrain IX
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Shall I that am as dust upon the plain
  Think with unloosened hurricanes to fight?
  Or shall I that was ravished from the night
Fall on the bosom of the night again?

poems.title: Quatrain X
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Endure! and if you rashly would unfold
  That manuscript whereon our lives are traced,
  Recall the stream which carols thro' the waste
And in the dark is rich with alien gold.

poems.title: Quatrain XI
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Myself did linger by the ragged beach,
  Whereat wave after wave did rise and curl;
  And as they fell, they fell--I saw them hurl
A message far more eloquent than speech:

poems.title: Quatrain XII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
We that with song our pilgrimage beguile,
  With purple islands which a sunset bore,
  We, sunk upon the sacrilegious shore,
May parley with oblivion awhile.

poems.title: Quatrain XIII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
I would not have you keep nor idly flaunt
  What may be gathered from the gracious land,
  But I would have you sow with sleepless hand
The virtues that will balance your account.

poems.title: Quatrain XIV
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The days are dressing all of us in white,
  For him who will suspend us in a row.
  But for the sun there is no death. I know
The centuries are morsels of the night.

poems.title: Quatrain XV
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
A deed magnanimous, a noble thought
  Are as the music singing thro' the years
  When surly Time the tyrant domineers
Against the lute whereoutof it was wrought.

poems.title: Quatrain XVI
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Now to the Master of the World resign
  Whatever touches you, what is prepared,
  For many sons of wisdom are ensnared
And many fools in happiness recline.

poems.title: Quatrain XVII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Long have I tarried where the waters roll
  From undeciphered caverns of the main,
  And I have searched, and I have searched in vain,
Where I could drown the sorrows of my soul.

poems.title: Quatrain XVIII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
If I have harboured love within my breast,
  'Twas for my comrades of the dusty day,
  Who with me watched the loitering stars at play,
Who bore the burden of the same unrest.

poems.title: Quatrain XIX
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
For once the witcheries a maiden flung--
  Then afterwards I knew she was the bride
  Of Death; and as he came, so tender-eyed,
I--I rebuked him roundly, being young.

poems.title: Quatrain XX
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Yet if all things that vanish in their noon
  Are but the part of some eternal scheme,
  Of what the nightingale may chance to dream
Or what the lotus murmurs to the moon!

poems.title: Quatrain XXI
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Have I not heard sagacious ones repeat
  An irresistibly grim argument:
  That we for all our blustering content
Are as the silent shadows at our feet.

poems.title: Quatrain XXII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Aye, when the torch is low and we prepare
  Beyond the notes of revelry to pass--
  Old Silence will keep watch upon the grass,
The solemn shadows will assemble there.

poems.title: Quatrain XXIII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
No Sultan at his pleasure shall erect
  A dwelling less obedient to decay
  Than I, whom all the mysteries obey,
Build with the twilight for an architect.

poems.title: Quatrain XXIV
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Dark leans to dark! the passions of a man
  Are twined about all transitory things,
  For verily the child of wisdom clings
More unto dreamland than Arabistan.

poems.title: Quatrain XXV
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Death leans to death! nor shall your vigilance
  Prevent him from whate'er he would possess,
  Nor, brother, shall unfilial peevishness
Prevent you from the grand inheritance.

poems.title: Quatrain XXVI
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Farewell, my soul!--bird in the narrow jail
  Who cannot sing. The door is opened! Fly!
  Ah, soon you stop, and looking down you cry
The saddest song of all, poor nightingale.

poems.title: Quatrain XXVII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Our fortune is like mariners to float
  Amid the perils of dim waterways;
  Shall then our seamanship have aught of praise
If the great anchor drags behind the boat?

poems.title: Quatrain XXVIII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Ah! let the burial of yesterday,
  Of yesterday be ruthlessly decreed,
  And, if you will, refuse the mourner's reed,
And, if you will, plant cypress in the way.

poems.title: Quatrain XXIX
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
As little shall it serve you in the fight
  If you remonstrate with the storming seas,
  As if you querulously sigh to these
Of some imagined haven of delight.

poems.title: Quatrain XXX
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Steed of my soul! when you and I were young
  We lived to cleave as arrows thro' the night,--
  Now there is ta'en from me the last of light,
And wheresoe'er I gaze a veil is hung.

poems.title: Quatrain XXXI
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
No longer as a wreck shall I be hurled
  Where beacons lure the fascinated helm,
  For I have been admitted to the realm
Of darkness that encompasses the world.

poems.title: Quatrain XXXII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Man has been thought superior to the swarm
  Of ruminating cows, of witless foals
  Who, crouching when the voice of thunder rolls,
Are banqueted upon a thunderstorm.

poems.title: Quatrain XXXIII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
But shall the fearing eyes of humankind
  Have peeped beyond the curtain and excel
  The boldness of a wondering gazelle
Or of a bird imprisoned in the wind?

poems.title: Quatrain XXXIV
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Ah! never may we hope to win release
  Before we that unripeness overthrow,--
  So must the corn in agitation grow
Before the sickle sings the songs of peace.

poems.title: Quatrain XXXV
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Lo! there are many ways and many traps
  And many guides, and which of them is lord?
  For verily Mahomet has the sword,
And he may have the truth--perhaps! perhaps!

poems.title: Quatrain XXXVI
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Now this religion happens to prevail
  Until by that religion overthrown,--
  Because men dare not live with men alone,
But always with another fairy-tale.

poems.title: Quatrain XXXVII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Religion is a charming girl, I say;
  But over this poor threshold will not pass,
  For I may not unveil her, and alas!
The bridal gift I can't afford to pay.

poems.title: Quatrain XXXVIII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
I have imagined that our welfare is
  Required to rise triumphant from defeat;
  And so the musk, which as the more you beat,
Gives ever more delightful fragrancies.

poems.title: Quatrain XXXIX
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
For as a gate of sorrow-land unbars
  The region of unfaltering delight,
  So may you gather from the fields of night
That harvest of diviner thought, the stars.

poems.title: Quatrain XL
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Send into banishment whatever blows
  Across the waves of your tempestuous heart;
  Let every wish save Allah's wish depart,
And you will have ineffable repose.

poems.title: Quatrain XLI
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
My faith it is that all the wanton pack
  Of living shall be--hush, poor heart!--withdrawn,
  As even to the camel comes a dawn
Without a burden for his wounded back.

poems.title: Quatrain XLII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
If there should be some truth in what they teach
  Of unrelenting Monkar and Nakyr,
  Before whose throne all buried men appear--
Then give me to the vultures, I beseech.

poems.title: Quatrain XLIII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Some yellow sand all hunger shall assuage
  And for my thirst no cloud have need to roll,
  And ah! the drooping bird which is my soul
No longer shall be prisoned in the cage.

poems.title: Quatrain XLIV
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Life is a flame that flickers in the wind,
  A bird that crouches in the fowler's net--
  Nor may between her flutterings forget
That hour the dreams of youth were unconfined.

poems.title: Quatrain XLV
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
There was a time when I was fain to guess
  The riddles of our life, when I would soar
  Against the cruel secrets of the door,
So that I fell to deeper loneliness.

poems.title: Quatrain XLVI
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
One is behind the draperies of life,
  One who will tear these tanglements away--
  No dark assassin, for the dawn of day
Leaps out, as leapeth laughter, from the knife.

poems.title: Quatrain XLVII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
If you will do some deed before you die,
  Remember not this caravan of death,
  But have belief that every little breath
Will stay with you for an eternity.

poems.title: Quatrain XLVIII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Astrologers!--give ear to what they say!
  "The stars be words; they float on heaven's breath
  And faithfully reveal the days of death,
And surely will reveal that longer day."

poems.title: Quatrain XLIX
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
I shook the trees of knowledge. Ah! the fruit
  Was fair upon the bleakness of the soil.
  I filled a hundred vessels with my spoil,
And then I rested from the grand pursuit.

poems.title: Quatrain L
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Alas! I took me servants: I was proud
  Of prose and of the neat, the cunning rhyme,
  But all their inclination was the crime
Of scattering my treasure to the crowd.

poems.title: Quatrain LI
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And yet--and yet this very seed I throw
  May rise aloft, a brother of the bird,
  Uncaring if his melodies are heard--
Or shall I not hear anything below?

poems.title: Quatrain LII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The glazier out of sounding Erzerûm,
  Frequented us and softly would conspire
  Upon our broken glass with blue-red fire,
As one might lift a pale thing from the tomb.

poems.title: Quatrain LIII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
He was the glazier out of Erzerûm,
  Whose wizardry would make the children cry--
  There will be no such wizardry when I
Am broken by the chariot-wheels of Doom.

poems.title: Quatrain LIV
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The chariot-wheels of Doom! Now, hear them roll
  Across the desert and the noisy mart,
  Across the silent places of your heart--
Smile on the driver you will not cajole.

poems.title: Quatrain LV
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
I never look upon the placid plain
  But I must think of those who lived before
  And gave their quantities of sweat and gore,
And went and will not travel back again.

poems.title: Quatrain LVI
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Aye! verily, the fields of blandishment
  Where shepherds meditate among their cattle,
  Those are the direst of the fields of battle,
For in the victor's train there is no tent.

poems.title: Quatrain LVII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Where are the doctors who were nobly fired
  And loved their toil because we ventured not,
  Who spent their lives in searching for the spot
To which the generations have retired?

poems.title: Quatrain LVIII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
"Great is your soul,"--these are the words they preach,--
  "It passes from your framework to the frame
  Of others, and upon this road of shame
Turns purer and more pure."--Oh, let them teach!

poems.title: Quatrain LIX
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
I look on men as I would look on trees,
  That may be writing in the purple dome
  Romantic lines of black, and are at home
Where lie the little garden hostelries.

poems.title: Quatrain LX
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Live well! Be wary of this life, I say;
  Do not o'erload yourself with righteousness.
  Behold! the sword we polish in excess,
We gradually polish it away.

poems.title: Quatrain LXI
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
God who created metal is the same
  Who will devour it. As the warriors ride
  With iron horses and with iron pride--
Come, let us laugh into the merry flame.

poems.title: Quatrain LXII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
But for the grandest flame our God prepares
  The breast of man, which is the grandest urn;
  Yet is that flame so powerless to burn
Those butterflies, the swarm of little cares.

poems.title: Quatrain LXIII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And if you find a solitary sage
  Who teaches what is truth--ah, then you find
  The lord of men, the guardian of the wind,
The victor of all armies and of age.

poems.title: Quatrain LXIV
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
See that procession passing down the street,
  The black and white procession of the days--
  Far better dance along and bawl your praise
Than if you follow with unwilling feet.

poems.title: Quatrain LXV
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
But in the noisy ranks you will forget
  What is the flag. Oh, comrade, fall aside
  And think a little moment of the pride
Of yonder sun, think of the twilight's net.

poems.title: Quatrain LXVI
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The songs we fashion from our new delight
  Are echoes. When the first of men sang out,
  He shuddered, hearing not alone the shout
Of hills but of the peoples in the night.

poems.title: Quatrain LXVII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And all the marvels that our eyes behold
  Are pictures. There has happened some event
  For each of them, and this they represent--
Our lives are like a tale that has been told.

poems.title: Quatrain LXVIII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
There is a palace, and the ruined wall
  Divides the sand, a very home of tears,
  And where love whispered of a thousand years
The silken-footed caterpillars crawl.

poems.title: Quatrain LXIX
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
And where the Prince commanded, now the shriek
  Of wind is flying through the court of state:
  "Here," it proclaims, "there dwelt a potentate
Who could not hear the sobbing of the weak."

poems.title: Quatrain LXX
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Beneath our palaces the corner-stone
  Is quaking. What of noble we possess,
  In love or courage or in tenderness,
Can rise from our infirmities alone.

poems.title: Quatrain LXXI
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
We suffer--that we know, and that is all
  Our knowledge. If we recklessly should strain
  To sweep aside the solid rocks of pain,
Then would the domes of love and courage fall.

poems.title: Quatrain LXXII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
But there is one who trembles at the touch
  Of sorrow less than all of you, for he
  Has got the care of no big treasury,
And with regard to wits not overmuch.

poems.title: Quatrain LXXIII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
I think our world is not a place of rest,
  But where a man may take his little ease,
  Until the landlord whom he never sees
Gives that apartment to another guest.

poems.title: Quatrain LXXIV
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Say that you come to life as 'twere a feast,
  Prepared to pay whatever is the bill
  Of death or tears or--surely, friend, you will
Not shrink at death, which is among the least?

poems.title: Quatrain LXXV
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Rise up against your troubles, cast away
  What is too great for mortal man to bear.
  But seize no foolish arms against the share
Which you the piteous mortal have to pay.

poems.title: Quatrain LXXVI
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Be gracious to the King. You cannot feign
  That nobody was tyrant, that the sword
  Of justice always gave the just award
Before these Ghassanites began to reign.

poems.title: Quatrain LXXVII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
You cultivate the ranks of golden grain,
  He cultivates the cavaliers. They go
  With him careering on some other foe,
And your battalions will be staunch again.

poems.title: Quatrain LXXVIII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The good law and the bad law disappear
  Below the flood of custom, or they float
  And, like the wonderful Sar'aby coat,
They captivate us for a little year.

poems.title: Quatrain LXXIX
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
God pities him who pities. Ah, pursue
  No longer now the children of the wood;
  Or have you not, poor huntsman, understood
That somebody is overtaking you?

poems.title: Quatrain LXXX
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
God is above. We never shall attain
  Our liberty from hands that overshroud;
  Or can we shake aside this heavy cloud
More than a slave can shake aside the chain?

poems.title: Quatrain LXXXI
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
"There is no God save Allah!"--that is true,
  Nor is there any prophet save the mind
  Of man who wanders through the dark to find
The Paradise that is in me and you.

poems.title: Quatrain LXXXII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The rolling, ever-rolling years of time
  Are as a diwan of Arabian song;
  The poet, headstrong and supremely strong,
Refuses to repeat a single rhyme.

poems.title: Quatrain LXXXIII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
An archer took an arrow in his hand;
  So fair he sent it singing to the sky
  That he brought justice down from--ah, so high!
He was an archer in the morning land.

poems.title: Quatrain LXXXIV
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The man who shot his arrow from the west
  Made empty roads of air; yet have I thought
  Our life was happier until we brought
This cold one of the skies to rule the nest.

poems.title: Quatrain LXXXV
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Run! follow, follow happiness, the maid
  Whose laughter is the laughing waterfall;
  Run! call to her--but if no maiden call,
'Tis something to have loved the flying shade.

poems.title: Quatrain LXXXVI
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
You strut in piety the while you take
  That pilgrimage to Mecca. Now beware,
  For starving relatives befoul the air,
And curse, O fool, the threshold you forsake.

poems.title: Quatrain LXXXVII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
How man is made! He staggers at the voice,
  The little voice that leads you to the land
  Of virtue; but, on hearing the command
To lead a giant army, will rejoice.

poems.title: Quatrain LXXXVIII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Behold the cup whereon your slave has trod;
  That is what every cup is falling to.
  Your slave--remember that he lives by you,
While in the form of him we bow to God.

poems.title: Quatrain LXXXIX
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The lowliest of the people is the lord
  Who knows not where each day to make his bed,
  Whose crown is kept upon the royal head
By that poor naked minister, the sword.

poems.title: Quatrain XC
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Which is the tyrant? say you. Well, 'tis he
  That has the vine-leaf strewn among his hair
  And will deliver countries to the care
Of courtesans--but I am vague, you see.

poems.title: Quatrain XCI
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The dwellers of the city will oppress
  Your days: the lion, a fight-thirsty fool,
  The fox who wears the robe of men that rule--
So run with me towards the wilderness.

poems.title: Quatrain XCII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Our wilderness will be the laughing land,
  Where nuts are hung for us, where nodding peas
  Are wild enough to press about our knees,
And water fills the hollow of our hand.

poems.title: Quatrain XCIII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
My village is the loneliness, and I
  Am as the travellers through the Syrian sand,
  That for a moment see the warning hand
Of one who breasted up the rock, their spy.

poems.title: Quatrain XCIV
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Where is the valiance of the folk who sing
  These valiant stories of the world to come?
  Which they describe, forsooth! as if it swum
In air and anchored with a yard of string.

poems.title: Quatrain XCV
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Two merchantmen decided they would battle,
  To prove at last who sold the finest wares;
  And while Mahomet shrieked his call to prayers,
The true Messiah waved his wooden rattle.

poems.title: Quatrain XCVI
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Perchance the world is nothing, is a dream,
  And every noise the dreamland people say
  We sedulously note, and we and they
May be the shadows flung by what we seem.

poems.title: Quatrain XCVII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Zohair the poet sang of loveliness
  Which is the flight of things. Oh, meditate
  Upon the sorrows of our earthly state,
For what is lovely we may not possess.

poems.title: Quatrain XCVIII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Heigho! the splendid air is full of wings,
  And they will take us to the--friend, be wise
  For if you navigate among the skies
You too may reach the subterranean kings.

poems.title: Quatrain XCIX
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Now fear the rose! You travel to the gloom
  Of which the roses sing and sing so fair,
  And, but for them, you'd have a certain share
In life: your name be read upon the tomb.

poems.title: Quatrain C
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
There is a tower of silence, and the bell
  Moves up--another man is made to be.
  For certain years they move in company,
But you, when fails your song do fail as well.

poems.title: Quatrain CI
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
No sword will summon Death, and he will stay
  For neither helm nor shield his falling rod.
  We are the crooked alphabet of God,
And He will read us ere he wipes away.

poems.title: Quatrain CII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
How strange that we, perambulating dust,
  Should be the vessels of eternal fire,
  That such unfading passion of desire
Should be within our fading bodies thrust.

poems.title: Quatrain CIII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Deep in a silent chamber of the rose
There was a fattened worm. He looked around,
Espied a relative and spoke at him:
It seems to me this world is very good.

poems.title: Quatrain CIV
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
A most unlovely world, said brother worm,
For all of us are piteous prisoners.
And if, declared the first, your thought is true,
And this a prison be, melikes it well.

poems.title: Quatrain CV
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
So well that I shall weave a song of praise
And thankfulness because the world was wrought
For us and with such providential care--
My brother, I will shame you into singing.

poems.title: Quatrain CVI
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
Then, cried the second, I shall raise a voice
And see what poor apologies are made.
And so they sang, these two, for many days,
And while they sang the rose was beautiful.

poems.title: Quatrain CVII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
But this affected not the songful ones,
And evermore in beauty lived the rose.
And when the worms were old and wiser too,
They fell to silence and humility.

poems.title: Quatrain CVIII
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
A night of silence! 'Twas the swinging sea
  And this our world of darkness. And the twain
  Rolled on below the stars; they flung a chain
Around the silences which are in me.

poems.title: Quatrain CIX
poems.author: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poems.text:
The shadows come, and they will come to bless
  Their brother and his dwelling and his fame,
  When I shall soil no more with any blame
Or any praise the silence I possess.
